title: Gregory of Nyssa's endless climb
hookLine: Moses climbing into darkness: the soul never stops growing toward God

cards: You finish something you've worked toward for years. The degree, the house, the marathon, the big project. A day or two later, a strange feeling often comes: a little emptiness.

Is that it? We tend to think the goal of anything is to arrive, and then rest. But in the 300s, a bishop in what's now Turkey looked at the life of Moses and came to a startling conclusion: with God, you never arrive.
And he thought that was the best news there is.

teach.h: FIRST LIGHT, THEN CLOUD, THEN DARKNESS.
teach.b: Gregory was bishop of a small town called Nyssa, in Cappadocia, in the late 300s. He came from a remarkable family: his older brother Basil and his sister Macrina are both honored as saints.

Near the end of his life, Gregory wrote The Life of Moses, reading the story as a map of the soul's journey to God. And he noticed the order of the story. First, Moses meets God in light, at the burning bush.
Later, God is a cloud leading the people. And at Sinai, it gets darker still.

teach.h: THE THICK DARKNESS WHERE GOD WAS.
teach.b: The King James Bible puts it simply: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Gregory says: that's the pattern.
The closer you get to God, the more you realize how far beyond you God is. Not because God hides, but because God has no edge. There's always more.

Later Moses asks to see God's glory, and he's allowed to see only God's back as he passes by. Gregory reads that beautifully: to see God is to follow behind him, always. For Gregory, this is joy, not frustration.
He taught that the very desire for God never runs out, because there's no end to what's desired.
Scholars call this idea epektasis, stretching forward. It comes from a line of Paul's: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before."
For Gregory, perfection isn't a finish line.
It's never stopping growing. So you're never too old, too late or too finished to take one more step toward the good.

how: Many Christians, especially in the Orthodox tradition, read Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses as a guide to prayer, and describe the spiritual life as endless growth toward God rather than a finished achievement.

games.q: Moses has met God in the fire, then in the cloud. on the mountain, what does he walk into?
games.why: Gregory read that darkness as closeness: the nearer you come, the more you see God has no edge.

practice: Think of one good thing you're already doing: being patient with someone, praying, giving, learning, getting stronger. Don't look back at how far you've come; picture only the next small step, not the whole mountain.
Let it feel like an invitation rather than a demand.

wordCard.voice: Epektasis, Gregory of Nyssa's word for stretching forward, reaching for more of God without ever arriving. The goal is not a finish line, but always growing.

orig.note: Greek: stretching out, reaching forward; the name scholars give Gregory's idea.

carryVoice: Your line: always further in. With God, there's always more. Two hundred sixty-five days in.
